hypothesis_test_result.scientific_significance: This is a clean single-variable (data-only) controlled experiment with an identical baseline. hypothesis_test_result.what_jp_err_actually_is: The ~0.45 jp_err is a FUNDAMENTAL policy-vs-reference trajectory mismatch that is NOT due to the reference data. Candidate root causes (for the NEXT single-variable direction, NOT this round): (1) the jp_err METRIC is phase-naive — it compares policy dof_pos against the reference at the episode frame index, but the policy's gait phase is unconstrained and NOT synchronized to the reference; a perfect-style walker at a different phase would still show large error. (2) The AMP style reward may be too weak vs the strong task-reward suite (tracking_lin_vel etc.) so the policy optimizes for stable walking, not reference-imitation (style_reward collapsed to 0 during training, same as baseline — the discriminator wins and the style signal vanishes). (3) eval commands vx=0.5 m/s while the reference walks ~1.3 m/s — different cadence => different joint trajectory even for good style imitation.

gateC_verdict: NOT PASSED (unchanged). jp_err fails (0.45>0.30, invariant to the data fix). The stability+walking-task groups remain STRONG and reproducible. Per §6/§11 no-threshold-lowering.

analysis_next_directions.primary: Re-examine the jp_err METRIC for phase-mismatch. A phase-naive frame-index comparison is the most likely culprit given the metric is invariant to a real data change. Test: compute a phase-ALIGNED jp_err (DTW or best-shift over a gait cycle) on the existing policy — this is a deterministic local re-analysis, no retrain needed. If phase-aligned jp_err drops near/below 0.30, the failure was a metric artifact, not a policy/imitation defect.
analysis_next_directions.secondary: If phase-aligned jp_err still fails: the policy is not imitating the reference. Direction = strengthen imitation signal (raise AMP style-reward weight / reduce task-reward scale) — but ONLY after the metric is validated, to avoid optimizing a broken metric.
